name: Ultrasonic skin treatment

lead: Ultrasonic skin treatment means applying ultrasound, usually through a handheld probe and a conductive gel or serum, to the skin of the face. People use it for a refreshed look: smoother-feeling skin and better absorption of skincare products.

Research on ultrasound and skin is substantial but mostly in other areas. Low-frequency ultrasound has been shown to raise skin permeability for drug delivery, and high-frequency ultrasound is used to image skin thickness and collagen structure.

paras: A probe is passed over the face with a gel or serum for a few minutes, in a clinic or with a home device, usually as part of a skincare routine. Users report the skin feeling smoother straight after.

Medical ultrasound used for permeation keeps skin permeable for hours to days in studies, and reviewers note that field intensity must be controlled to avoid harmful bioeffects. Consumer devices vary widely; people with implants, active skin conditions or pregnancy typically check with a clinician.

chain: Ultrasound applied with gel or serum
angle.text: Users apply ultrasound probes with serums to make skin feel smoother and products absorb better. The permeability effect is documented in lab and clinical settings; cosmetic outcomes are mainly user-reported.

lead: Ultrasonic skin treatment covers facials and devices that apply ultrasound waves to the skin, typically with a gel or serum. People use them to leave the skin feeling smoother and to help skincare products penetrate.

The scientific literature on ultrasound and skin is largely about drug delivery. A review of transdermal ultrasound reported that the technique offers promise for needle-free delivery and that acoustic intensity and exposure time need careful quantification to balance safety and efficacy [1]. In ten healthy volunteers, sonication with the SonoPrep device sharply increased skin permeability, which lasted up to 48 hours without occlusion [2]. Other work uses high-frequency ultrasound to image skin thickness and collagen organisation [3][4].

paras: Ultrasound facials use mechanical sound vibrations, delivered through a probe, to act on the skin surface. Therapeutic ultrasound in general works through thermal effects from absorbed sound and non-thermal effects such as cavitation and acoustic streaming [5].

Low-frequency ultrasound can increase skin permeability. Reviews describe it as a method for needle-free drug delivery, with the stratum corneum as the main barrier it overcomes [1]. In a study of ten adults, sonicated forearm skin stayed highly permeable for the full 48 hours without occlusion, and recovered more quickly than under occlusion [2]. Therapeutic ultrasound is also used with medication gels in phonophoresis [5].

High-frequency ultrasound is used to image the skin. A 1984 report introduced a scanner that measured full skin thickness and visualised subcutaneous fat and muscle [4]. Ex vivo work linked ultrasonic backscatter and attenuation to collagen fibre distribution in human dermis [3].

No studies found on cosmetic ultrasound facials specifically. Clinical studies of ultrasonic skin permeation devices in volunteers have measured permeability and skin impedance, including a trial showing lower skin impedance with SonoPrep than with two conventional skin-prep methods [6].
Reviewers stress accurate measurement of the acoustic field to avoid harmful bioeffects [1].

timeline.event: A high-resolution ultrasonic skin scanner is described for measuring skin thickness [4].
